cvEn:
Avraham (Avon) Kesev, son of Batya and Ezra, was born in 1928 in Aleppo, in northern Syria. He attended a people's school and a vocational school run by the Alliance network, and joined a semi-underground Zionist youth movement. In 1941, before reaching his bar mitzvah, Avon set out on foot with friends for Eretz Israel. He succeeded in crossing the border and reaching the country.

At the age of 16 he was accepted into the Notrim (the Jewish Supernumerary Police), and served in Kiryat Motzkin, in the Haifa area, and in the Western Galilee. In 1943 he "added" years to his age and enlisted as a volunteer in a Hebrew transport unit of the British Army, which was later attached to the Jewish Brigade. During his service with the Brigade he managed, dressed in British Army uniform, to visit his family in his birthplace of Aleppo, in Syria. To his worried and proud parents he told of the plans to establish the state that was coming, and urged them to join him and make aliyah. After his discharge from the Brigade, Avon enlisted in the Palmach, and when the War of Independence broke out he served with the 7th Battalion of the Palmach, taking part in operations in the Haifa area and escorting convoys to Jerusalem. With the Egyptian invasion he was transferred to the southern front.

During the battles of Ashdod, three companies of the 7th Battalion of the Palmach's Negev Brigade, with the support of a jeep company, attacked the southern concentration of enemy forces in Ashdod. The force moved at night from the direction of Nitzanim and ran into difficulties of movement because of the sand dunes. At dawn on 25 Iyar 5708 (3 June 1948) contact was made with the enemy, who opened fire on the Palmach force, causing many casualties among our forces, including Avraham Kesev, who was hit by a burst of bullets in his abdomen. The force withdrew in daylight toward Nitzanim, carrying the wounded with it and conducting combat as it retreated. When it was no longer possible to evacuate the wounded from the battlefield, ten soldiers, Kesev among them, were left behind in the field. At his request his comrades left him a rifle and a hand grenade for self-defense. About two hours after the battle, his comrades returned to collect those who remained in the field. Some were buried immediately, while the others, Avraham Kesev among them, who was buried under a wrong name, were only brought to burial a year and a half later, following a search initiated by some of the families of the fallen and by the army.

On his last day, in the face of the bloody fighting, Avraham wrote a last letter and sent it to his brother, but it was lost on the way. He was almost twenty years old when he fell. He left behind parents and seven brothers and sisters. For 56 years Avraham Kesev was considered a fallen soldier whose burial place was unknown, until the IDF's missing-persons unit located his grave in the Nahalat Yitzhak cemetery, where he had been buried under a wrong name. On 25 Iyar 5764 (16 May 2004) a military headstone unveiling ceremony was held, attended by members of Avraham Kesev's family.
